summary: Defines two LDAP attributes, vendorName and vendorVersion, that a directory server may place in its root entry to say which software it is. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A directory server can post a sign on its front door saying who made it and which version it is. This defines those two sign fields.

questions: how to find ldap server vendor
subtitle: How LDAP servers advertise their vendor and version

tldr.problem: LDAP clients need a way to discover what vendor made an LDAP server and what version of that software is installed, to identify and work around known implementation issues.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3045 defines two optional LDAP attributes, vendorName and vendorVersion, that a directory server can place in its root DSE (the root entry) to advertise this information.
tldr.outcome: Directory servers can now publish their vendor identity and version, allowing client software to identify specific server implementations and apply workarounds when needed.

today: RFC 3045 is an Informational document and remains the specification for LDAP vendor identification attributes. While not all LDAP servers implement these attributes, those that do follow this RFC. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) is a system for accessing directory information, like a phone book for the internet. When an LDAP client connects to a server, it can query the root DSE (Directory Server Entry) to discover information about that server, such as what controls and extensions it supports.

This RFC adds two new attributes that servers can place in the root DSE: vendorName (the name of the company that wrote the server) and vendorVersion (the release version number of that software).
sections.plainLanguage: When you connect to an LDAP server, it is like knocking on a door. The server can tell you who runs the building and what version of the locks they have installed.

sections.title: The Two Attributes
sections.content:
vendorName is a single text field containing the name of the LDAP server implementer, such as 'Novell, Inc.' or another vendor. It is optional and read-only, meaning clients cannot modify it. All LDAP server implementations SHOULD maintain this attribute.

vendorVersion contains a string representing the version of the LDAP server software, such as 'LDAPv3 8.0' or similar version numbers used by the software developer. Like vendorName, it is single-valued, read-only, and optional. The version string MUST be unique between different versions, but vendors can format it however they choose.
sections.plainLanguage: vendorName is like the company logo on the front door. vendorVersion is the version number, like '3.0' or '2.1'.

sections.title: Using Vendor Information
sections.content:
Software often has bugs or incomplete features. It is impossible to catalog every known issue in the standard LDAP attributes. When clients discover a known issue with a particular version of a server, they can use vendorName and vendorVersion to identify that exact version and apply a workaround.

However, these attributes MUST NOT be used to discover or advertise features. Feature discovery should use proper LDAP mechanisms, preferably ones defined alongside those features. Many server implementations support multiple platforms and configurations, so bugs may only affect certain setups. Clients SHOULD accept any value in these attributes and MUST assume a server is correct if they do not recognize the vendor or version.
sections.plainLanguage: If a programmer finds a quirk in version 3.5 of a directory server, they can tell their software, 'When you see this vendor and version, do this workaround.'

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
These attributes are provided only for display, information, and anomaly identification. The mere presence of vendor and version information does not guarantee that the server was actually built by that vendor or that the version is authentic. A misconfigured or compromised server could report false information.

Server implementers should be aware that this information could be misused to target security exploits. An attacker who learns that a server is running a specific version with a known vulnerability can attempt to exploit it. However, the RFC itself does not introduce new security issues beyond those already present in LDAP.
sections.plainLanguage: A server could lie about who made it or what version it is. Bad people might use this information to find servers with known problems and attack them.

sections.title: Notes for Implementers
sections.content:
Server implementers SHOULD maintain accurate vendorName and vendorVersion attributes. Developers may consider tying the vendorVersion to the build mechanism so it is automatically updated when the version number changes.

Client developers must remember that vendorName and vendorVersion are NOT mechanisms for feature discovery. Clients written to accept any value in these attributes, and to assume a server is complete and correct if they do not recognize it, will be more robust and compatible with diverse LDAP implementations. Clients MUST work with servers that do not publish these attributes at all.
sections.plainLanguage: Server makers should keep this information up to date. Client makers should not rely on it to figure out what the server can do—they should ask the server directly about its features.
